'''''Monotropa hypopitys''''', [[Synonymy (taxonomy)|syn.]] '''''Hypopitys monotropa''''', also known as '''yellow bird's nest''' in Britain and Ireland,<ref>{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.82szng |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref> '''pinesap''' and '''false beechdrops''' in Canada and the United States,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hypopitys monotropa Crantz - Database of Vascular Plants of Canada (VASCAN) |url=http://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/5527 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250317091221/http://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/5527 |archive-date=2025-03-17 |access-date=2025-11-10 |website=data.canadensys.net |language=en}}</ref> is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] of the [[Monotropoideae]] subfamily of the family [[Ericaceae]]. It is native to temperate regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/plant-profile/MOHY3 |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=plants.sc.egov.usda.gov}}</ref><ref name="Beatty-2011">{{Cite journal |last1=Beatty |first1=Gemma E. |last2=Provan |first2=Jim |date=April 2011 |title=High clonal diversity in threatened peripheral populations of the yellow bird's nest (Hypopitys monotropa; syn. Monotropa hypopitys) |journal=Annals of Botany |language=en |volume=107 |issue=4 |pages=663–670 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcr003 |issn=1095-8290 |pmc=3064538 |pmid=21257715}}</ref> and is scarce within its range.<ref name="Beatty-2011" /> ''M. hypopitys'' is a [[Mycotroph|mycotrophic]] plant which means it obtains nutrients and fixed carbon by [[Parasitism|parasitizing]] the [[Mycorrhizal network|mycorrhizal networks]] of trees.<ref name="fs.usda.gov">{{Cite web |title=What are they? |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/beauty/mycotrophic/whatarethey.shtml |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref> It lacks chlorophyll and does not photosynthesize.<ref name="wildflower.org">{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=MOHY3 |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref> The species name, ''M. hypopitys'', is from [[Latin|Latinized]] [[Greek language|Greek]] hypo-, "under", and pitys, "pine", referring to where it often grows.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Monotropa hypopitys {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/163883-2 |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=www.ipni.org}}</ref> 

[[File:Monotropa hypopithys 9686.JPG|left|thumb|The pink to cream flower, with four to five petals, is borne on a short stalk.]]
[[File:Monotropa hypopitys 0319.JPG|right|thumb|''Monotropa hypopitys'' in [[Henry M. Jackson Wilderness]], Washington]]
==Physical description==
''M. hypopitys'' is a fleshy dicot that grows to {{Convert abbreviated|10-35|cm}} tall. True stems are nonexistent; instead, the only part which emerges from the soil are unbranched, adventitious [[Inflorescence|inflorescences]] developmentally similar to [[adventitious roots]]. The [[Bract|bracts]] are 5–10 mm long scale-like structures, which cover most of the inflorescence. It has cosexual flowers that are [[pendulous]] when young, but become erect when they begin to mature into the [[fruit]] which is a [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beatty |first1=Gemma E. |last2=Provan |first2=Jim |date=April 2011 |title=High clonal diversity in threatened peripheral populations of the yellow bird's nest (Hypopitys monotropa; syn. Monotropa hypopitys) |journal=Annals of Botany |language=en |volume=107 |issue=4 |pages=663–670 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcr003 |issn=1095-8290 |pmc=3064538 |pmid=21257715}}</ref> Flowers are 9–12 mm long and produced in a cluster of 1–11 together at the apex of the [[raceme]] inflorescence. The seeds are very small, weighing only 0.000003 of a gram. ''M. hypopitys'' has several color morphs, including yellow, red, and yellowish-white.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Monotropa hypopitys |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/beauty/mycotrophic/monotropa_hypopitys.shtml |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref> It is frequently mistaken for a fungus due to its unique, fungus-like physical characteristics.<ref name="fs.usda.gov" />

== Parasitism ==
Unlike autotrophs, [[Mycotroph|mycotrophs]] like ''Monotropa hypopitys'', cannot make their own food. Instead, they exploit the mutualism between mycorrhizal networks and trees.<ref name="fs.usda.gov" /> By penetrating fungal hyphae, ''M. hypopitys'' siphons off resources. ''M. hypopitys'' often parasitizes the hyphae associated with [[oak]] and [[pine]] trees.<ref name="wildflower.org" /> It also displays host specificity for ''[[Tricholoma]]'' fungi.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Johansson |first1=V. A. |last2=Bahram |first2=M. |last3=Tedersoo |first3=L. |last4=Kõljalg |first4=U. |last5=Eriksson |first5=O. |date=2017 |title=Specificity of fungal associations of Pyroleae and Monotropa hypopitys during germination and seedling development |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/mec.14050 |journal=Molecular Ecology |language=en |volume=26 |issue=9 |pages=2591–2604 |doi=10.1111/mec.14050 |pmid=28173637 |bibcode=2017MolEc..26.2591J |issn=1365-294X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Monotropa hypopitys'' is the most widespread member of its subfamily (Monotropoideae). Outside of North America, its wide distribution includes India, China, Pakistan, Russia, and much of Europe.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bombay Natural History Society. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/188343 |title=The journal of the Bombay Natural History Society |last2=Society |first2=Bombay Natural History |date=2009 |publisher=Bombay Natural History Society |volume=v.106:no.1 (2009:Apr.) |location=Bombay}}</ref> In the United States, the heath family (Ericaceae) mycotrophic species are most common in the western mixed coniferous forests.<ref name="fs.usda.gov" /> ''M. hypopitys'' distribution is influenced by the host distribution, specifically that of ''Tricholoma'' fungi. <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leake |first1=J. R. |last2=McKendrick |first2=S. L. |last3=Bidartondo |first3=M. |last4=Read |first4=D. J. |date=2004 |title=Symbiotic germination and development of the myco-heterotroph Monotropa hypopitys in nature and its requirement for locally distributed Tricholoma spp. |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1469-8137.2004.01115.x |journal=New Phytologist |language=en |volume=163 |issue=2 |pages=405–423 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.2004.01115.x |pmid=33873615 |bibcode=2004NewPh.163..405L |issn=1469-8137|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Reproductive ecology and phenology ==
''M. hypopitys'' flowering [[phenology]] typically ranges from April to December but is dependent on the geographic region and flower morph.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wildflower Search |url=https://wildflowersearch.org/search |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=wildflowersearch.org}}</ref><ref name="Klooster-2009">{{Cite journal |last1=Klooster |first1=Matthew R. |last2=Culley |first2=Theresa M. |date=2009 |title=Comparative analysis of the reproductive ecology of Monotropa and Monotropsis: Two mycoheterotrophic genera in the Monotropoideae (Ericaceae) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3732/ajb.0800319 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=96 |issue=7 |pages=1337–1347 |doi=10.3732/ajb.0800319 |pmid=21628282 |bibcode=2009AmJB...96.1337K |issn=1537-2197|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Its two dominant color forms, red and yellow, have non-overlapping reproductive phenologies. The yellow form blooms in mid-summer while the red morph is known to flower in the fall.<ref name="Klooster-2009" /> While both forms are [[Self-incompatibility|self-compatible]], the yellow form has higher rates of [[Autogamy|autogamous]] reproduction.<ref name="Klooster-2009" /> [[Pollinator]] diversity within the ''Monotropa'' genus is low with bumblebees being the predominant pollen dispersal agent.<ref name="Klooster-2009" /> The red and yellow morphs also have distinct floral systems with the red form displaying [[Herkogamy|approach herkogamy]]. The yellow form is devoid of the spatial separation of reproductive structures associated with herkogamy. <ref name="Klooster-2009" />

== Evolutionary history ==
''M. hypopitys'' non-photosynthetic nature is attributed to its significantly reduced chloroplast genome.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gruzdev |first1=Eugene V. |last2=Mardanov |first2=Andrey V. |last3=Beletsky |first3=Alexey V. |last4=Kochieva |first4=Elena Z. |last5=Ravin |first5=Nikolai V. |last6=Skryabin |first6=Konstantin G. |date=2016-01-01 |title=The complete chloroplast genome of parasitic flowering plant Monotropa hypopitys: extensive gene losses and size reduction |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/23802359.2016.1155090 |journal=Mitochondrial DNA Part B |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=212–213 |doi=10.1080/23802359.2016.1155090 |pmc=7800667 |pmid=33473455}}</ref> When it was originally classified, only two species, ''M. hypopitys'' and ''[[Monotropa uniflora|M. uniflora]],'' made up the ''Monotropa'' genus.<ref name="Liu-2017">{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Zhen-Wen |last2=Zhao |first2=Qian-Ru |last3=Peng |first3=Hua |last4=Zhou |first4=Jing |date=2017 |title=(2545) Proposal to conserve the name Hypopitys (Ericaceae) with a conserved type |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.12705/664.20 |journal=Taxon |language=en |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=987–988 |doi=10.12705/664.20 |bibcode=2017Taxon..66..987L |issn=1996-8175|hdl=11336/84412 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Recent analysis of morphological characteristics and genetic information suggests that ''M. hypopitys'' is more closely related to the other members of the Monotropoideae subfamily than it is to ''M. uniflora''.<ref name="Liu-2017" />
